summary: Describes the state of standardization of Internet protocols as determined by the IAB. It is historic and was replaced by RFC 1360.

eli5.summary: It is an old scoreboard of which Internet rules were official. A newer scoreboard replaced it.

questions: what is the iab official protocol standards list
how did the internet standards process work in 1992
subtitle: The IAB's official list of Internet protocol standards and their status.

tldr.problem: Internet protocol developers and users need a single authoritative source that lists which protocols are standards, which are still being tested, and which have been superseded.
tldr.mechanism: The IAB publishes this memo quarterly to list protocols and their standardization state (Standard, Draft Standard, Proposed Standard, Experimental, Informational, or Historic) and requirement level (Required, Recommended, Elective, Limited Use, or Not Recommended).
tldr.outcome: This document became a Historic standard and was replaced by RFC 1360 to reflect the changing Internet standards landscape.

facts.value: 6 (Standard, Draft Standard, Proposed Standard, Experimental, Informational, Historic)

facts.value: 5 (Required, Recommended, Elective, Limited Use, Not Recommended)

today: RFC 1360 replaced this document. RFC 1280 is Historic and documents the IAB's protocols standards process as it was defined in early 1992.

sections.title: The Purpose and Process
sections.content:
RFC 1280 is the Internet Activities Board's (IAB) official registry of protocol standards. It explains both the maturity levels of protocols—how far along they are in standardization—and their requirement levels, which indicate how widely they should be adopted.

The document lists protocols in six categories: Standard protocols that are officially approved and assigned STD numbers; Draft Standard protocols under active IAB consideration; Proposed Standard protocols being reviewed for future standardization; Experimental protocols for research use only; Informational protocols from other sources like vendors; and Historic protocols that have been superseded or are no longer in use.
sections.eli5: The IAB keeps a list of which Internet rules are official, which are being tested, and which are too old to use. Each protocol gets labeled so engineers know whether they must use it, should use it, or can pick something else.

sections.title: Maturity Levels and Requirement Levels
sections.content:
A protocol's maturity level (or state) describes its progress through standardization. The path typically goes from Proposed Standard, requiring at least two independent implementations, through Draft Standard, which signals that standardization is likely, to full Standard status. The IAB enforces minimum delays of 6 months between transitions to allow community review.

The requirement level (or status) is independent of maturity and describes how widely a protocol should be used. Required protocols must be implemented in all systems; Recommended protocols should be implemented; Elective protocols are optional; Limited Use protocols apply only in special circumstances; and Not Recommended protocols should be avoided.
sections.eli5: Each protocol has two labels. One says how tested it is: Proposed (still new), Draft Standard (likely to pass), Standard (approved), or Experimental (just for research). The other says how much you need to use it: Required (everyone must), Recommended (you should), Elective (your choice), Limited (special cases only), or Not Recommended (avoid it).

sections.title: The Standards Track
sections.content:
The standards track is the formal path a protocol follows toward standardization. Only the Internet Engineering Steering Group (IESG) of the IETF and the IAB can move a protocol along this path. A protocol may take many months or years to move from Proposed Standard through Draft Standard to Standard, with minimum waiting periods enforced at each step.

A protocol can also exit the track into the Experimental state, or move to Historic status if it becomes obsolete. The RFC text includes a state-machine diagram showing all possible transitions, with double-boxed states (Standard and Historic) being long-term and single-boxed states (Proposed and Draft Standard) being temporary.
sections.eli5: Protocols follow a path like climbing a mountain: you start at the bottom (Proposed), climb to Draft Standard, and reach the peak as a Standard. The climb takes months and needs proof that the protocol works. Once you reach the top you can stay there for years. If the protocol becomes outdated, it moves to Historic instead.

sections.title: The RFC Process and Standards System
sections.content:
All Internet standards must be published as RFCs, but not all RFCs are standards. The RFC Editor publishes standards documents only with approval from both the IESG and the IAB. Experimental documents are notified to the IESG and may be reviewed by relevant working groups. Once published with an RFC number, a document never changes; if a protocol is revised, it gets a new RFC number.

RFC 1280 established how the IAB and IETF would manage protocol evolution. The document assigned STD numbers to official standards and provided clear categorization that persisted through subsequent editions.
sections.eli5: The Internet has one main rule for publishing: no RFC can be changed after it is published. If you need to fix a protocol, you write a new RFC. This document explained how standards get published and who decides which protocols are official.

sections.title: Status and Usage Today
sections.content:
RFC 1280 defined the standards landscape as of March 1992. It established how the IETF and IAB would manage protocol evolution and set definitions that persisted through several editions. The document assigned STD numbers to official standards and provided clear rules for what constitutes the Internet protocol suite.

RFC 1360 replaced this document with an updated version that reflected the growing protocol ecosystem and refinements to the standards process. This RFC is now Historic and serves primarily as a historical record of how the standards system was defined in its early years.
sections.eli5: This document created the official system for ranking Internet protocols. It was important at the time but got replaced with newer versions as the Internet grew and the standards process improved. It is now Historic, which means it is outdated but documented for history.
